headline: AI fakes a growing problem on Apple Books, some ‘written’ in a few hours
summary: AI-generated fake books are proliferating on Apple Books, with some reportedly created in just a few hours. This trend raises concerns for authors and readers alike.
details: Tech writer Joanna Stern recently discovered 10 fake versions of her book, "I Am Not a Robot," listed on Apple Books. These AI-generated titles mimic her work, highlighting a growing problem on the platform.

Some of these fraudulent books are reportedly "written" in just a few hours using AI tools. This rapid production rate makes it difficult for platforms to keep up and for authors to protect their intellectual property.

The proliferation of AI fakes not only impacts authors' livelihoods but also diminishes trust in digital bookstores. Readers risk purchasing low-quality or plagiarized content, eroding the value of legitimate works.

Apple Books, like other digital publishing platforms, faces the challenge of implementing effective measures to detect and remove AI-generated content. This issue underscores the broader ethical and practical dilemmas posed by generative AI.

headline: 1 in 8 apps for US troops ship Chinese/Russian code, raising data harvesting concerns
summary: A new study reveals hundreds of apps marketed to US military personnel contain code from foreign nations, including Huawei and Yandex, posing significant national security risks through potential data harvesting.
details: A recent study found that over one in eight mobile apps marketed to US military personnel contain software built by companies in China, Russia, or other foreign nations. This raises fresh concerns that adversary governments could harvest data revealing where service members live, work, and deploy.

Researchers from Purdue University, the US Military Academy at West Point, and Florida International University identified Huawei code in a popular app used by service members to rate base living conditions. Two other apps incorporated the Russian ad service Yandex.

The largely unregulated advertising industry often tracks civilians and service members similarly. However, exposed location data can reveal troop deployments, unit movements, and routines within sensitive intelligence facilities where nuclear weapons are believed to be stored.

The US Central Command confirmed in April that it received multiple threat reports of adversaries exploiting commercial location data to target or surveil American personnel in the Middle East. This marks the first official confirmation of troops being hunted through the data-broker economy.

The new study specifically examined over 220 military-focused apps from the Google Play store and military subreddits. Nearly two-thirds, or 64%, contained third-party code known as SDKs, typically used for analytics and advertising, which can track user behavior and locations.

Forty percent of the apps collected or shared more data than they disclosed in their Google or Apple store listings. While most common SDKs were from Google and Facebook, 76 unique SDKs were found, with roughly 7% originating from nations considered adversarial by the Pentagon.

Twelve of the apps contained Huawei's HMS Core, a software kit capable of mapping user locations and storing data. Researchers observed no data actively going to Huawei servers, but an SDK can be updated remotely at any time, potentially turning dormant code into spyware.

A survey of 103 military-affiliated Americans, including active-duty service members and veterans, revealed that over 83% used at least one app engaging in data practices they found uncomfortable. This highlights a widespread privacy concern among those serving.
